title: Evolving Together, Failing Apart:The Skill–Policy Co-evolution Trap in Self-Improving Agents

paper.title: Evolving Together, Failing Apart: The Skill–Policy Co-evolution Trap in Self-Improving Agents
paper.abstract:
Abstract Skill–policy co-evolution—in which an agent’s policy model and its skill bank improve each other
during training—is a promising paradigm for self-improving agents.
Current evaluations score the co-evolved policy on the final bank it trained with (the delivered bank ).
After deployment, however, skills may be rewritten, added or removed more frequently than the policy model is retrained, leaving the policy to operate on a drifted skill bank that neither the training objective nor existing evaluation protocols address.
In this paper, we first establish, through theoretical and empirical analysis, that the fragility hidden by this blind spot is not incidental.
The acceptance rule these methods share ( cooperative acceptance ) ties a policy’s competence to the bank it co-evolved with, leaving it fragile once skills drift, regardless of the implementation;
empirically, sensitivity to skill drift grows as co-evolution training proceeds.
We therefore introduce the CO -evolution D rift A udit ( CODA ), a
deployment-oriented evaluation protocol that simulates skill drift and, alongside success rate under worst-case drift, introduces two new metrics: a consistency rate under meaning-preserving edits and a resistance rate to corrupted skills.
Across four co-evolution methods and five benchmarks (six settings), worst-case success is 5–13 points below the peak measured for each delivered pair, erasing 52–93% of the delivered bank’s gain over the no-skill baseline. CODA thus reframes the target of co-evolution—from peak performance on the co-evolved bank to the ability to harness skills however they evolve—and provides a shared standard against which future methods can be audited.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Building agents that improve themselves is a central goal of current agent research, and co-evolving a skill library with a policy is one of the most promising routes ( Xia et al., 2026a ; He et al., 2026 ) . The agent solves tasks, distills the experience into reusable skills, and uses those skills to strengthen its policy in turn, so competence compounds over rounds. A recent line of methods ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Lin et al., 2026 ) follows exactly this recipe: it iterates the policy and the skill bank together during training and reports large gains on agent benchmarks. Each ultimately delivers a pair—a co-evolved policy and its final skill bank (the delivered bank )—and reports the policy’s task success on that bank. However, current evaluation is disconnected from deployment: it assumes that the skill bank remains fixed after training. Real skill banks are non-stationary: skills are rewritten, entries are added or removed, and versions coexist, often changing faster than the policy is retrained. A deployed policy therefore typically runs on a bank that has drifted from the one it was delivered with, yet existing protocols do not test whether performance is maintained. A few works note this brittleness ( Liu et al., 2026d ; Hebbar et al., 2026 ) but offer neither a systematic measurement nor a causal account. We argue that the blind spot conceals a property of the training objective, not an incidental evaluation artifact. Co-evolution repeatedly adapts the policy and bank into a mutually specialized pair, while evaluation rewards exactly that pairing. The policy is therefore optimized for its delivered bank rather than for transferable skill use. We establish this in two ways. Theoretically, we prove that the shared acceptance rule—retaining a skill update only when it helps the current policy—places the delivered pair at a peak over candidate banks, so rewriting the delivered skills cannot improve the policy and usually degrades its performance (Section 2 ). Empirically, using the proposed co-evolution fragility curve , we show that sensitivity to skill drift increases as training proceeds in five of six settings (Section 3 ). We call this the co-evolution trap (Figure 1 ): the process that raises peak performance also creates sensitivity to bank drift. Figure 1: The skill–policy co-evolution trap (conceptual illustration) . (1) Training : The policy and skill bank co-evolve round by round, and evaluation reports the peak reached by the resulting delivered pair. (2) Deployment : The skill bank continues to evolve while the policy remains fixed. Because the policy is specialized to its delivered bank, its performance degrades as the bank drifts. (3) Goal : An ideally co-evolved policy that retains its performance as skills evolve. Establishing the problem exposes a second gap: existing evaluations cannot measure it, because they report only one success rate on the fixed delivered bank. We therefore introduce the CO -evolution D rift A udit ( CODA ), a deployment-oriented protocol for auditing post-deployment skill drift under controlled conditions. CODA supplements the conventional peak success rate with worst-case success and two new metrics—a consistency rate under meaning-preserving edits and a resistance rate to corrupted skills. Across four methods and five benchmarks (six settings), worst-case success is 5–13 points below the peak measured for each delivered pair, erasing 52–93% of the delivered bank’s gain over the no-skill baseline, so the reported peak overstates the competence a deployment can rely on. CODA thus reframes the target of co-evolution—from achieving peak performance on the bank a method co-evolved with to using skills reliably as they keep changing—and we release it as a common standard for auditing future methods. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We expose a trap in skill–policy co-evolution : current evaluations measure fit to a fixed delivered bank, leaving performance under deployment-time bank change unmeasured. • We theoretically and empirically demonstrate its mechanism and signature: under cooperative acceptance and candidate coverage, no covered rewrite improves the delivered policy; empirically, 18/18 endpoint pairs obey this prediction and fragility grows along training in five of six settings. • We propose a deployment-oriented evaluation protocol , CODA, reporting worst-case success under tested content-level drift, consistency under meaning-preserving edits, and resistance to corrupted skills, making the deployment robustness of the delivered policy–bank pair measurable.

sections.heading: Problem setting.
sections.text: A task x x is drawn from a distribution D D , a skill bank S S lies in a space 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , and a policy π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , S ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,S) maps both to a distribution over action sequences, with skills entering as text in its context. Methods optimize and report the expected return J ( θ , S ) = 𝔼 x ∼ D [ R ( π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , S ) ) ] , J(\theta,S)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}\!\left[R\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,S)\right)\right], (1) where R R is a binary success indicator, so J J is the reported success rate. We fold skill selection into π θ \pi_{\theta} , making J J a function of the bank as a whole. Co-evolution alternates a policy step , which improves θ \theta against the current bank, and a bank step , which proposes banks by rewriting, adding or removing skills and retains one through an acceptance test. After T T rounds, it delivers ( θ ∗ , S ∗ ) (\theta^{*},S^{*}) and reports J ⁡ ( θ ∗ , S ∗ ) J(\theta^{*},S^{*}) as its peak return —the de facto objective for comparing these methods.

Second, their gates favor banks that serve the current policy, whether through reward thresholds, sampled-return comparisons or posteriors over competing versions. sections.heading: Scope.
sections.text: Neither proposition assumes a particular model class, task distribution or reward; both apply to any method whose delivered pair satisfies Assumptions 1 and 2 (proofs in Appendix D ). Under analogous coverage, reversing the selection preference drives Φ \Phi down instead (Appendix D.5 ), so the selection bias—not co-evolution alone—governs whether robustness emerges. The magnitude and training-time evolution of Φ \Phi are examined empirically in Section 3.2 .

sections.heading: 3.1 A Five-Axis Skill-Drift Probe
sections.text: To measure the response set of Definition 2 , we perturb the delivered skill bank while holding the task and policy fixed. Five axes represent increasingly structural forms of drift. T1 (semantic) rewrites a skill synonymously, changing wording but preserving meaning. T2 (sufficiency) deletes necessary steps or injects irrelevant content, leaving the skill on topic but incomplete. T3 (misleading) replaces the prescribed strategy with an incorrect one. T4 (ecosystem) changes bank composition by adding, removing or mixing skill versions. T5 (autonomy) removes the bank entirely. T1–T3 alter existing skill content and lie within ℬ ⁡ ( S ∗ ) \mathcal{B}(S^{*}) ; T4 and T5 are reported as structural diagnostics outside it. Figure 3 illustrates all five axes; Appendix F provides detailed examples. Figure 3: The five-axis probe on one ALFWorld task. Each row applies a single operator to the delivered bank and reports its effect on the same skill text, with the edit marked in red. T1–T3 alter selected skill content under fixed retrieval and lie within ℬ ⁡ ( S ∗ ) \mathcal{B}(S^{*}) ; T4 changes bank composition, and T5 removes the bank. The task and policy remain fixed, and outcomes are schematic. An external language model produces the variants from domain- and axis-specific prompts. For T1–T3, retrieval runs once on the original bank and only the selected content fields are replaced, preventing retrieval changes from confounding content changes. T4 and T5 alter bank composition by design. Full prompts, parameters, examples and masking details are in Appendices E , F and E.5 .

sections.heading: 3.2 Tracing Fragility Along Co-evolution
sections.text: A two-point comparison between the base and delivered policies is difficult to compare across settings because base performance ranges from near zero to substantial. We instead trace checkpoints along one training trajectory while holding the delivered bank S ∗ S^{*} and its perturbed variants fixed. The policy checkpoint is therefore the only changing component. This design yields our proposed co-evolution fragility curve , a within-run longitudinal diagnostic of whether fragility grows with co-evolution. Where available, the base ( s0 ) checkpoint anchors the left endpoint; because it did not co-evolve with S ∗ S^{*} , positive responses remain admissible under Proposition 1 . We retain checkpoints from the start of the run through its peak unperturbed success rate. Later checkpoints are not larger doses of successful co-evolution, whereas local training dips within the retained segment remain included (Appendix H ).

sections.heading: Absolute and normalized readings.
sections.text: We track each axis with two numbers. The absolute drop ( Drop \mathrm{Drop} ; larger means more fragile) is the performance lost at a given checkpoint, Drop a ​ ( t ) = SR ⁡ ( S ∗ ) − SR ⁡ ( S a ∗ ) , \mathrm{Drop}_{a}(t)\;=\;\mathrm{SR}(S^{*})-\mathrm{SR}(S^{*}_{a}), (7) where SR ⁡ ( S ∗ ) \mathrm{SR}(S^{*}) is the unperturbed success rate of checkpoint t t and SR ⁡ ( S a ∗ ) \mathrm{SR}(S^{*}_{a}) is its success rate under the axis- a a perturbation. The retention performance ( RP \mathrm{RP} ; higher is better) is competence-normalized, RP a ​ ( t ) = SR ⁡ ( S a ∗ ) SR ⁡ ( S ∗ ) , \mathrm{RP}_{a}(t)\;=\;\frac{\mathrm{SR}(S^{*}_{a})}{\mathrm{SR}(S^{*})}, (8) so checkpoints of different ability compare on one scale (retaining 90% of the score gives RP = 0.9 \mathrm{RP}=0.9 whether the baseline is 30% or 80%). Reporting both rules out the objection that a larger drop merely reflects more headroom, which retention normalizes away. Figure 4: Co-evolution fragility curve for ReSkill on ALFWorld. Left: unperturbed success rate over the analyzed (rising) segment of training. Right, top row: absolute drop per axis; right, bottom row: retention performance RP \mathrm{RP} per axis. Competence keeps rising (left) while the policy grows more sensitive to perturbation of its own bank— Drop \mathrm{Drop} trends upward and its normalized counterpart RP \mathrm{RP} downward—so co-evolution buys peak performance at the cost of fragility. A minimal linear–Gaussian construction shows analytically that rising competence and fragility can emerge from the same co-evolution process (Appendix D.3 ).

sections.heading: Experimental setup.
sections.text: We evaluate four skill–policy co-evolution methods over six method–environment settings: SkillRL ( Xia et al., 2026a ) on ALFWorld ( Shridhar et al., 2020 ) and WebShop ( Yao et al., 2022 ) ; ReSkill ( He et al., 2026 ) on ScienceWorld ( Wang et al., 2022 ) and ALFWorld; Evolving-RL ( Fan et al., 2026 ) on Mind2Web ( Deng et al., 2023 ) ; and ARISE ( Li et al., 2026 ) on DeepScaleR-AMC23 ( Luo et al., 2025 ) . They share only the selection bias abstracted by Assumption 1 , so a trend common to all four tracks the paradigm rather than one implementation. Appendix G details method- and benchmark-specific configurations.

sections.heading: Training trend.
sections.text: The result is consistent across four methods and five benchmarks: as co-evolution training proceeds, the policy grows more capable with its own skill bank but increasingly sensitive to changes in it (Figure 4 ). Unperturbed success rises from the first to the final retained anchor in all six settings, including 5.2 % → 88.8 % 5.2\%\to 88.8\% for SkillRL -ALFWorld, 16.4 % → 25.2 % 16.4\%\to 25.2\% for Evolving-RL -Mind2Web and 15.5 % → 87.4 % 15.5\%\to 87.4\% for ARISE -AMC23. At least one content-level axis has a significantly positive Drop \mathrm{Drop} slope in five of six settings; across the eighteen axis–setting pairs, twelve are significant—four on each of T1, T2 and T3. The effect is therefore not confined to misleading skills: semantic and sufficiency perturbations also become costlier in multiple settings. The final delivered checkpoint is fragile in three concrete ways. (i) The one-sided prediction holds (18/18): no content-level rewrite beats evaluation noise in any of the eighteen axis–setting pairs, as Proposition 1 predicts. (ii) The losses are substantial: a meaning-preserving rewrite alone costs 10.9 10.9 points on ReSkill -ScienceWorld (peak 50.3 % 50.3\% ). (iii) The bank still helps under drift: SR min \mathrm{SR}_{\min} stays above the no-skill anchor in all six settings, so the failure is lost bank-derived gains, not negative skill value. Full results are reported in Appendix H : per-anchor grids in Tables 8 – 13 , heat maps in Figures 5 – 10 , and the remaining fragility curves in Figures 11 – 15 . The within-run trend and these delivered-pair results show one specialization pattern across distinct methods and domains; the next section turns this dependence into CODA, a checkpoint-free audit of any delivered policy–bank pair.

sections.heading: 4 CODA: Auditing Co-evolved Policies for Skill Drift
sections.text: The previous two sections established, theoretically and empirically, that co-evolution leaves a policy fragile once its skills drift. What the field lacks, however, is not another method—new update rules or acceptance tests—but a way to measure the failure: a shared standard that scores how well a delivered policy holds up when its bank changes, comparably across methods. We therefore introduce CODA, a protocol that audits the one artifact every method ships—a co-evolved policy and its delivered bank—and reports its robustness to skill drift on a common footing.

sections.heading: 4.1 Design and the Shared Rewriting Suite
sections.text: CODA audits only the delivered pair—a co-evolved policy and its delivered bank—plus the shared suite, and assigns scores only to quantities with a predefined direction, so the metric set stays closed; the design rationale (checkpoint-freeness, the direction-first rule, and why diagnostics such as the surface-form ratio κ \kappa of Appendix H.5 are excluded) is in Appendix E . The suite is the part of this paper meant to outlive it, under one hard rule: rewriting is performed by the released suite, not by the party under evaluation —an evaluation whose conditions the evaluated party controls is not an evaluation. For the content-level axes T1–T3, retrieval is run once on the unperturbed bank and only the content of the selected skills is rewritten; the suite pins the rewriting model and its sampling, releases the perturbed banks rather than a script, preserves bank structure, and reports the edit strength it produced. The five requirements (R1–R5) that make this workable, with their full rationale, are in Appendix E.2 .

The no-skill condition anchors the gate and resistance criterion rather than constituting a score (Appendix E.8 ). sections.heading: 4.3 Verdict: An Absolute, Within-Method Pass or Fail
sections.text: CODA’s verdict is an absolute pass or fail, judged within a single method: it passes when the gate clears ( Δ net > 0 \Delta_{\mathrm{net}}>0 ), the consistency rate stays within the CR 0 \mathrm{CR}_{0} noise band, and every harmful axis satisfies Eq. ( 12 ). Every check reads a method against its own numbers, never against another’s; our headline—that the reported peak conceals a much lower worst case—therefore ranks nothing and needs no cross-method comparison. Ranking is a use we leave to adopters: once some pass, SR min \mathrm{SR}_{\min} is the natural leaderboard key, and three raw quantities are published regardless—the peak, the no-skill rate, and the per-axis perturbed rates. Auditing each method on the bank it produced is a deliberate choice, not a concession: a robustness protocol standardizes the operator and its budget, not the perturbation text, and no shared bank exists in deployment anyway. The full argument—including why a bank too vague to corrupt is caught by the gate—is in Appendix E.9 .

sections.text: We audit four co-evolution methods across the six method–environment settings of Section 3.3 , running CODA on each final delivered pair—not any intermediate checkpoint—with perturbed banks from the shared rewriting suite. sections.heading: The reported peak overstates deployable competence.
sections.text: Across all six settings the worst-case success rate under content-level drift trails the peak by 4.9–12.6 points (about 5–13): 4.9 on Evolving-RL -Mind2Web, 5.0 on SkillRL -WebShop, 6.5 on ARISE -AMC23 and 10.2–12.6 on the other three. Only the peak is customarily reported. Because the absolute drop scales with how much the bank helps, we normalize by that headroom: drift consumes 52–93% of the skill benefit in every setting. The worst-case rate nonetheless stays above the no-skill baseline throughout, so the failure is not that skills hurt but that most of the advertised gain is contingent on the bank’s exact wording and disappears once it drifts. What a deployment can rely on is therefore nearer this worst case than the peak, by the majority of the benefit skills appear to add.

sections.heading: The worst case is often the mildest change.
sections.text: In three of the six settings the T1 (meaning-preserving) rate falls below the harsher T2 and T3 rates (e.g. SkillRL -ALFWorld 78.6 vs. 79.3/79.5), costing up to 12.6 points relative to the peak ( ReSkill -ALFWorld 76.9 → \to 64.3)—evidence that the policy has overfit to the bank’s phrasing rather than its meaning. The consistency rate makes the churn explicit: at 77.5 77.5 – 87.0 87.0 it sits below its noise floor CR 0 = 91.9 \mathrm{CR}_{0}=91.9 – 94.4 94.4 , so 13 13 – 23 % 23\% of tasks flip outcome under a meaning-preserving rewrite, against 6 6 – 8 % 8\% under decoding noise alone; the consistency criterion therefore fails in every setting—and with it the verdict—while the net-benefit gate and the harmful-axis criterion pass. CODA does not declare these methods useless: it quantifies how much of each reported peak is co-evolved with the delivered bank, precisely the quantity current evaluation leaves unmeasured.

sections.heading: Skill–policy co-evolution.
sections.text: A growing family of methods co-evolves a skill library with the policy, including SkillRL ( Xia et al., 2026a ) , ReSkill ( He et al., 2026 ) , Skill1 ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , ARISE ( Li et al., 2026 ) , SAPO ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , and SkillMaster ( Yang et al., 2026a ) . These methods differ in update cadence, library growth, validation gates, and skill injection (Table 1 ), yet share the same evaluation premise: the co-evolved policy is tested on its delivered bank. We introduce no new member of this family; instead, we examine this shared premise and its consequences under deployment-time skill drift.

sections.heading: Agent robustness under skill drift.
sections.text: Robustness evaluations for language agents typically perturb the task side of the interaction—instructions, observations, tool outputs, or environment dynamics. We instead perturb the agent’s own procedural knowledge, which task-side benchmarks treat as fixed. Recent work documents that skill libraries drift and that agent performance can degrade accordingly ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ) , that skills may harm rather than help ( Tank and Nama, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) , and that self-evolution is not always faithful ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Lv et al., 2026 ) . Other approaches repair skills post hoc or construct more drift-tolerant skills ( Liu et al., 2026c ; Park et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2026 ) ; by contrast, we audit the delivered policy’s dependence on whichever bank it encounters. This setting also resembles zero-shot coordination ( Hu et al., 2020 ) , with the skill bank acting as a co-evolved partner that may change after training. Appendix B provides further discussion.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: This work shifts the evaluation of skill–policy co-evolution from performance on a single delivered pair to robustness under realistic deployment-time skill drift. Our analysis identifies cooperative acceptance as a source of dependence on the co-evolved bank, while the co-evolution fragility curve shows that this dependence can strengthen over training. CODA operationalizes these findings by auditing whether a delivered policy remains consistent under benign rewrites and resists incomplete or misleading skills. The delivered peak is therefore informative but insufficient: future methods should preserve its gains while learning to interpret, reject, and adapt to skills as the bank evolves.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: Large language models play two distinct roles in this work. As a component of the method , the CODA rewriting suite calls gpt-4o-2024-08-06 (temperature 0.7 0.7 , with version and sampling parameters pinned as specified in Appendix E ) to generate the perturbed skill banks that serve as evaluation stimuli; because these banks are released, reproducing our evaluation does not require re-running the model. As an authoring aid , LLMs assisted only with language polishing, grammar, and style. All research questions, methodology, experiments, analyses, and conclusions were conceived, implemented, and verified by the authors, who take full responsibility for the content of this paper.

sections.heading: Ethics statement
sections.text: The CODA suite deliberately produces incomplete (T2) and misleading (T3) procedural instructions in order to measure how a delivered policy withstands skill drift. These corrupted skills are generated and consumed entirely within the benchmark harness, are never deployed or shown to real users, and are released alongside the suite so that their content is transparent and auditable. The work involves no human participants, collects no personally identifiable information, and introduces no new sensitive data; we see no direct risks to privacy, fairness, or legal compliance, and the work complies with the ICLR Code of Ethics.

sections.heading: Reproducibility statement
sections.text: We take several concrete measures to make our results reproducible. • Rewriting suite and protocol: the rewriting model, its version, and all sampling parameters are pinned (Section 4.1 ), and the domain contexts, layered prompts, and resulting perturbed banks are released, so the evaluation can be reproduced without re-running the generative model. • Environments and data: all benchmarks used (ALFWorld, WebShop, ScienceWorld, Mind2Web, and DeepScaleR-AMC23) are publicly available; the test splits, episode counts, and evaluation configuration are documented in Section 4.4 and Appendix G , together with the released configuration. Together, these measures allow independent researchers to reproduce our results and verify the claims made in this paper.

sections.heading: Appendix A Limitations
sections.text: We note three limitations of this work. L1 Rewriting is not bit-reproducible. A language model rewriting a skill is not a deterministic operator: pinned model versions, pinned sampling, and released perturbed banks reduce the variance a re-runner faces but do not remove it. If the bank was written by the same model family that later rewrites it, the measured fragility may be optimistically low. L2 We diagnose but do not fix. We expose the fragility and provide a measurement tool, but propose no mitigation. The natural direction is the distributional objective of Eq. ( 6 )—training against a distribution of bank perturbations rather than a single fixed bank—but turning it into a practical method, and keeping the net-benefit gate satisfied, is future work. L3 Scale is unstudied. Whether broader exposure—more benchmarks, larger banks, more data—reduces sensitivity to wording or merely raises the peak from which the worst case falls away is beyond our design, and is the most interesting open question beyond the fix itself.

sections.heading: Skill–policy co-evolution.
sections.text: A growing family of methods lets an agent distill task experience into reusable skills and then trains the policy on the enlarged bank ( Liu et al., 2026a ; Zou et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Feng et al., 2026 ) . SkillRL ( Xia et al., 2026a ) distills successful trajectories into skills that are added to a monotonically growing library and gated by reward on sampled rollouts. ReSkill ( He et al., 2026 ) caps the library at a fixed size and uses Thompson sampling to decide which incumbent a new candidate should replace. Skill1 ( Shi et al., 2026 ) jointly optimizes the policy and bank end-to-end, admitting skills from trajectories that already succeed. ARISE ( Li et al., 2026 ) evolves a two-tier hierarchy of intrinsic skills under a hierarchical reward. SAPO ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) admits a skill only when its estimated marginal utility to the current policy is positive. SkillMaster ( Yang et al., 2026a ) lets the policy itself score candidates, retaining high-scoring ones into a managed library. These methods differ in cadence, library growth, validation gate, and injection mechanism (Table 1 ; Appendix C gives the full classification). What they do not differ in is how success is reported: the co-evolved policy is run on the delivered bank and a task success rate is given. Surveys chart this space ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2026 ) , and recent variants push co-evolution to test-time ( Mao et al., 2026 ) , self-play ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , and deployment-time meta-learning ( Xia et al., 2026b ) . We contribute no new member of this family. Our object of study is the family itself—specifically, the one premise that survives all of their design disagreements.

sections.heading: Agent robustness and adversarial co-evolution.
sections.text: Work on robustness for language agents perturbs the task side of the interaction—instructions, observations, tool outputs, environment dynamics—and asks whether performance survives. We perturb a different thing: the agent’s own store of procedural knowledge, which no task-side benchmark touches because it is normally treated as part of the agent rather than part of the environment. Concurrently, a cluster of works documents that skill libraries drift and that agents degrade under that drift ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ) , that skills can hurt as often as they help ( Tank and Nama, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) , and that self-evolution is not always faithful ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Lv et al., 2026 ) . These diagnose the symptom; none ties it to the co-evolution objective or measures it on the delivered artifact. SkillRevise ( Liu et al., 2026c ) repairs skills post hoc, and GenDa ( Park et al., 2026 ) with programmatic skill induction ( Shao et al., 2026 ) build drift-tolerant skills from the skill side; we instead audit the policy’s dependence on whatever bank it is handed. The closest conceptual relative is zero-shot coordination ( Hu et al., 2020 ) , where a policy trained with one partner must act with another it never co-evolved with; our setting is the single-agent analog, with the skill library in the role of the partner that changed. A separate line evolves an adversary alongside the learner, in game-theoretic heuristic discovery ( Ke et al., 2026 ) or attacker–defender safety training ( Wen et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2025 ) , and reports robustness gains . This is not a counterexample to Proposition 1 but a confirmation of its premise read in reverse: those methods accept a candidate precisely when it lowers the current policy’s return, so the sign in Assumption 1 is flipped and the conclusion flips with it. Appendix D.5 works this through, and the comparison is instructive rather than competitive: it locates the fragility in the acceptance rule rather than in co-evolution as such.

sections.heading: Standardized perturbation suites.
sections.text: CODA belongs to a tradition of fixed perturbation suites applied to models their designers did not build: corruption benchmarks in vision ( Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019 ) and behavioral test suites in NLP ( Ribeiro et al., 2020 ) both consist of a released operator, a reporting convention, and the finding that published systems fail more than their headline numbers suggest. We follow that template on the skill side. One difference must be stated rather than glossed over: those operators are deterministic algorithms that reproduce bit-for-bit, whereas rewriting a skill with a language model does not. We narrow the gap: we pin the rewriting model, its version and its sampling parameters; we ship the domain context so nothing is left to the user; and we release the perturbed banks alongside the suite (Section 4.1 ). We do not close it, though— Section 6 lists it first among the limitations.

sections.heading: Appendix C Classification of Existing Methods
sections.text: The four axes of Table 1 are defined as follows. Update cadence determines how the two steps interleave, from strictly alternating through near-synchronous to jointly optimized. The validation gate determines how a candidate bank is admitted: no test at all, an improvement test on sampled rollouts, or a posterior test such as Thompson sampling. Library growth is either monotone, so that skills accumulate, or capped, so that admission displaces an incumbent. The injection mechanism determines what reaches the context at inference: a batch selected by task category, or a small subset triggered per step. We now place each surveyed method on these axes and state its acceptance rule—the property that Assumption 1 abstracts. In every case the gate admits a candidate bank only when it does not lower (and usually strictly raises) the current policy’s return, however differently that test is implemented. • SkillRL ( Xia et al., 2026a ) : alternating cadence, monotone growth, batch top- k k injection. A distilled skill is admitted whenever it does not reduce reward on sampled rollouts and is never removed thereafter, so the retained bank is the reward-non-decreasing one. • ReSkill ( He et al., 2026 ) : near-synchronous cadence, library capped at eight, per-step injection. A candidate is validated by Thompson sampling and kept only if its posterior return improves on the incumbent it would displace. • SAPO ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) : near-synchronous cadence, two-tier capped growth, reranked injection. A skill enters only when its estimated marginal utility to the current policy is positive. • Skill1 ( Shi et al., 2026 ) : joint optimization, monotone growth, log-probability injection. Skills are distilled from trajectories that already succeed ( r = 1 r{=}1 ) and trained jointly with the policy, so what is retained is exactly what supported a return the policy did not lose. • ARISE ( Li et al., 2026 ) : joint optimization, two-tier growth, log-probability injection. Intrinsic skills are evolved under a hierarchical reward and retained on improvement of that reward. • SkillMaster ( Yang et al., 2026a ) : near-synchronous cadence, policy-managed growth and injection. The policy itself scores candidate skills and retains the high-scoring ones, i.e. those that raise its own return. • Evolving-RL ( Fan et al., 2026 ) : joint optimization, monotone growth, batch injection. A skill is admitted end-to-end when it clears a reward threshold on the current policy. • COSPLAY ( Wu et al., 2026 ) : near-synchronous cadence, lifecycle-managed growth, per-step injection. Skills pass a contract-verification step and are retained over their lifecycle while they continue to serve the policy’s return. The gates differ in form—an improvement test on rollouts, a Thompson posterior, a marginal-utility check, a reward threshold, a policy score, a contract—but all favor skills that serve the current policy. Assumption 1 idealizes this shared selection bias. Proposition 1 is model-agnostic but additionally requires the candidate-coverage condition of Assumption 2 ; it therefore applies conditionally rather than automatically to the eight surveyed methods.

sections.heading: E.1 Design Principles
sections.text: Two principles guide the protocol. Checkpoint-free : CODA uses only the delivered pair plus the shared suite, because step definitions are not comparable across methods, many releases keep only the final checkpoint, and prompt-based evolution has no notion of a step at all; the fragility curve of Section 3.2 therefore serves as causal evidence in this paper, not a protocol metric. Direction-first : each metric’s direction is stated before its formula, and any quantity without a defined direction serves as a gate rather than a score, as T5 does. The metric set is thus closed: diagnostics without a defined direction, such as the surface-form dependence ratio κ \kappa of Appendix H.5 , are excluded from the report card.

sections.heading: E.2 Requirements on the Rewriting Suite (R1–R5)
sections.text: Five requirements make the hard rule of Section 4.1 —that rewriting is performed by the released suite, not by the party under evaluation—workable across methods with incomparable bank formats. The remaining subsections of this appendix specify each in implementable detail. • R1 Selection masking: retrieval is run once on the unperturbed bank and only the content of the selected skills is substituted (Appendix E.5 ). • R2 Field-classification interface: a method declares which fields arew retrieval-side (frozen) and which are content (rewritable), rather than standardizing a bank format. • R3 Reproducibility: the rewriting model, its version and its sampling are pinned, and the perturbed banks—not a script—are released (Appendix E.4 ). • R4 Structural checks, not a semantic verifier: only declared content fields may change and the bank structure is preserved; meaning-preservation is left to the released banks for inspection, not to a similarity threshold, and is validated in Appendix H.6 . • R5 Strength reporting: the suite reports the edit distance and similarity it produced, the analog of stating an attack budget.

sections.heading: E.3 Perturbation Operators
sections.text: A skill σ \sigma is a record of typed fields, partitioned into a retrieval-side part ρ ⁡ ( σ ) \rho(\sigma) —the fields a method uses to decide when the skill is surfaced, such as its title, trigger conditions, keywords and usage statistics—and a content part γ ⁡ ( σ ) \gamma(\sigma) , the procedural text the policy reads once the skill is in context. A bank is a finite set S = { σ 1 , … , σ n } S=\{\sigma_{1},\dots,\sigma_{n}\} , and each axis is an operator on banks. The content-level axes T1–T3 keep the set of skills fixed and rewrite only content fields, so their image lies in the neighborhood ℬ ⁡ ( S ∗ ) \mathcal{B}(S^{*}) of Definition 1 . Writing g a g_{a} for the layered-prompt rewriter of Appendix E.4 applied field-by-field to the declared content fields, with ρ ⁡ ( σ ) \rho(\sigma) copied verbatim: • T1 (semantic) replaces γ ⁡ ( σ ) \gamma(\sigma) by a meaning-preserving paraphrase g 1 ​ ( γ ​ ( σ ) ) g_{1}(\gamma(\sigma)) : the wording changes, the prescribed behavior does not. • T2 (sufficiency) replaces γ ⁡ ( σ ) \gamma(\sigma) by g 2 ​ ( γ ​ ( σ ) ) g_{2}(\gamma(\sigma)) that stays on topic but no longer suffices, either by deleting a required step or by injecting irrelevant material. • T3 (misleading) replaces γ ⁡ ( σ ) \gamma(\sigma) by g 3 ​ ( γ ​ ( σ ) ) g_{3}(\gamma(\sigma)) that is well-formed but prescribes an incorrect strategy. The structural axes T4–T5 change which skills are present and therefore lie outside ℬ ⁡ ( S ∗ ) \mathcal{B}(S^{*}) : • T4 (ecosystem) applies a sequence of composition edits—insert a new skill, delete an incumbent, or replace a skill by an alternative version—leaving the text of every surviving skill unchanged. • T5 (autonomy) removes the bank entirely, T 5 ​ ( S ) = ∅ T_{5}(S)=\varnothing .

sections.heading: E.4 Layered Rewriting Prompt
sections.text: Section 3.1 states that skill rewrites are produced by gpt-4o-2024-08-06 at temperature 0.7 0.7 . This appendix expands the prompt architecture that anchors the rewriter in each benchmark’s semantics.

sections.heading: Why a layered prompt.
sections.text: Handing a skill to a general-purpose model with a single rewriting instruction risks two failure modes: the output may reference actions or objects that do not exist in the environment, and the edit may drift from the intended axis (e.g. a T1 “paraphrase” that silently removes a step, which is T2 territory). A layered prompt prevents both by supplying the domain context the model lacks and restricting the scope of the edit.

sections.heading: Architecture.
sections.text: The prompt is assembled from five layers (Table 3 ). Layers 1–4 are shared across all content-level axes and fix everything the rewrite must respect—the environment, the tokens that must survive verbatim, the task category and the skill’s capability tag. Only the fifth layer carries the axis directive, so one shared skeleton plus one swapped instruction produces every content-level variant. The user turn supplies the specific skill field to be rewritten.

sections.heading: Field-level targeting.
sections.text: Each axis declares which fields it may touch and the remainder are copied verbatim. T1, for instance, rewrites a skill’s principle and when_to_apply and the description , why and how of a recorded mistake, while titles and identifiers are left unchanged—ensuring that retrieval-side metadata is never accidentally altered.

sections.heading: T4 and T5.
sections.text: The ecosystem (T4) and autonomy (T5) axes are structural operations on the bank (adding, removing or replacing skills, or removing the bank entirely) rather than text rewrites, and do not use this prompt. Since the same prompt need not return the same text twice, the banks we evaluated against are released alongside the suite and are the reproducible artifact. Because the surfaced set is Sel i \mathrm{Sel}_{i} in both the unperturbed and the perturbed condition, any change in outcome is attributable to the rewritten content rather than to a different set of skills being retrieved, and coverage is identical across methods regardless of bank size. This constancy of the selection map on ℬ ⁡ ( S ∗ ) \mathcal{B}(S^{*}) is also what licenses folding selection into π θ \pi_{\theta} in Section 2 , so that J J can be treated as a function of the bank as a whole. Masking applies only to T1–T3. The structural axes T4 and T5 change which skills exist by design, so retrieval is re-run against the modified bank and the selected set is not held fixed; by Definition 1 these axes fall outside ℬ ⁡ ( S ∗ ) \mathcal{B}(S^{*}) , and the propositions of Section 2 make no claim about them.

sections.heading: E.6 Field-Classification Interface
sections.text: An adopter declares, once per bank format, which fields the suite may rewrite ( content ) and which must remain untouched ( retrieval-side ). The content fields are the target of T1–T3; the retrieval-side fields determine which skills are selected and must be frozen so that performance changes can be attributed to content alone (Section 3.1 ). Two examples from this paper: Format Content (rewritable) Retrieval-side (frozen) SkillRL principle , example name , keywords , embedding ReSkill strategy task_type , score , embedding The declaration is a one-line JSON mapping; the suite validates it at run time and refuses to rewrite a field classified as retrieval-side.

sections.heading: E.7 Quality Control and Strength Reporting
sections.text: Three checks run automatically, and it is worth being exact about what they do and do not establish. Field targeting. Each axis declares the fields it may rewrite and the remainder are copied verbatim. T1, for instance, rewrites a skill’s principle and when_to_apply and the description , why and how of a recorded mistake, while titles and identifiers are untouched. Length band. The tier instruction asks for a rewrite within ± 30 % \pm 30\% of the original length; enforcement is looser, rejecting a field only when the ratio of rewritten to original length falls outside [ 0.5 , 2.0 ] [0.5,2.0] . A rejected field is regenerated once, and the second attempt is accepted whatever its length. Separately, the pipeline retries on transport failures with exponential backoff; those retries are unrelated to quality and are not a check. Structural validation of the misleading axis. The T3 banks are verified after generation to contain the same skill identifiers in the same order and the same number, to leave titles and when_to_apply unchanged, to have modified every principle , and to leave the recorded mistakes alone. This establishes that the edit landed where it was supposed to land, not that the resulting strategy is wrong. No check tests meaning. There is no embedding-similarity threshold, no entailment test for T1 and no verification that a T3 variant genuinely prescribes an incorrect strategy; requirement R4 (Appendix E.2 ) gives the reasoning, and the released banks are what a reader inspects instead.

sections.heading: Strength reporting (R5).
sections.text: For each released perturbed bank, the suite logs two perturbation-strength statistics per skill: (a) the character-level edit distance between the original and rewritten text, normalized by the original length, and (b) the cosine similarity of sentence embeddings (all-MiniLM-L6-v2) between the original and rewritten versions. These distributions are released alongside the perturbed banks so that adopters can verify the perturbation intensity falls within the intended range for each axis. The suite additionally records the prompt-share statistic : the fraction of the inference prompt occupied by injected skill text, which contextualizes how much of the input the policy relies on from the bank.

sections.heading: Why T4 and T5 are reported but not scored.
sections.text: T5 (autonomy) has no defined direction: removing the bank may hurt because it held knowledge the policy could not internalize, or because it held strategies the policy should have absorbed, and the number alone cannot tell these apart; the no-skill condition therefore serves as the anchor for the gate and the resistance criterion rather than as a score. T4 (ecosystem) is not the same operator across methods—bank sizes differ by an order of magnitude, from tens or hundreds of skills to a cap of eight—so it is reported (Section 3 , Appendix H ) but excluded from the score, regardless of whether its effect is larger or smaller than the content-level axes in a given setting.

sections.heading: Consistency and its noise floor.
sections.text: The consistency criterion tests CR \mathrm{CR} against a two-standard-deviation band around CR 0 \mathrm{CR}_{0} , the agreement between two unperturbed runs, which fixes the repeat-level noise floor. Rather than tabulate the per-setting standard deviations, we read the outcome from the flip rates directly: CR 0 \mathrm{CR}_{0} corresponds to a 6 6 – 8 % 8\% flip rate between two unperturbed evaluations—the churn attributable to decoding randomness alone—whereas the T1 rewrite flips 13 13 – 23 % 23\% of task outcomes, two to three times that floor. This gap exceeds repeat-level evaluation noise in every setting, so CR \mathrm{CR} sits below the band and the consistency criterion fails throughout. The per-episode logs needed to recompute CR \mathrm{CR} and CR 0 \mathrm{CR}_{0} are released with the suite.

sections.heading: Logging requirements.
sections.text: The identities above and McNemar’s test on Eq. ( 12 ) all read paired binary outcomes at the level of individual tasks. An adopter therefore must log, for every evaluation condition (unperturbed, T1, T2, T3, and ∅ \varnothing ) and every repeat, the per-episode indicator c i ∈ { 0 , 1 } c_{i}\in\{0,1\} together with the task identifier i i . Two consequences follow: • Common task set. The no-skill condition, the unperturbed condition, and each axis- a a condition must be evaluated on the same N N task identifiers. Aggregating a success rate on a slightly different task subset breaks RR a \mathrm{RR}_{a} and the McNemar statistic, since the pairing no longer holds task-by-task. • Aggregated scores are not sufficient. A report card that publishes only SR \mathrm{SR} per condition, without per-episode outcomes, is not auditable: neither CR \mathrm{CR} , RR a \mathrm{RR}_{a} nor the McNemar p p can be recomputed from it. The suite therefore requires per-episode logs alongside the aggregated report card, and its reference implementation writes them out by default.

sections.heading: E.9 Auditing Each Method on Its Own Bank
sections.text: Section 4.3 states that CODA audits each method on the bank it delivered rather than on a shared bank, and gives a one-paragraph summary of why. The complete argument runs to four points. First, the unit of evaluation is the artifact the method delivers. The bank is not an external test condition supplied by us; it is half of what the method produced. Auditing method A on A’s bank measures exactly what A would deploy, whereas forcing every method onto a shared bank measures a configuration nobody ships. A shared-bank protocol would therefore answer a different question: how well does each method run on a piece of text it did not choose. That is a reasonable question, but it is not a robustness question about the delivered system. Second, what a robustness protocol standardizes is the operator and the budget, not the perturbation. Projected gradient descent produces a different adversarial example for every model because it uses that model’s gradients, and no one calls the comparison unfair: what is fixed is the attack—its algorithm and its budget—not the resulting pixel. CODA is isomorphic. The rewriting instructions, the rewriting model, and the coverage—the set of skills actually retrieved for each task—are all fixed; the resulting text differs because the banks differ. The obligation this introduces is stated as R5: the strength actually applied to each method must be reported, so that unequal severity is visible rather than deniable. Third, the obvious way to game the protocol does not work. A method could try to survive rewriting by shipping a bank so vague that corrupting it changes nothing. But a bank vague enough to be uncorruptable is almost always vague enough to be useless, and that shows up immediately in the gate of Eq. ( 9 ): a method that clears the gate has published a bank with real content, and one that fails the gate does not qualify. The two requirements pull against each other—benefit demands that the bank carry real content, robustness demands that the policy not depend on its exact wording—and a method must satisfy both with a single artifact. Fourth, deployment fidelity points the same way. There is no shared bank in the real world: each deployment owns a library that changes on its own schedule, for reasons internal to that deployment. Perturbing each method’s own bank is the faithful simulation of that situation. A shared bank would be the distortion, not the fair comparison, because it evaluates every method under a configuration none of them would have deployed.

sections.heading: Appendix G Experimental Configuration
sections.text: This appendix expands the setup summarized in Section 3.3 .

sections.heading: Method and benchmark diversity.
sections.text: The four methods spread across Table 1 rather than clustering in one corner of it: they differ in the update schedule, the bank growth policy, the admission rule and the injection mechanism, sharing only the current-policy selection bias abstracted by Assumption 1 . The benchmarks are equally spread, spanning embodied interaction (ALFWorld), shopping (WebShop), scientific procedures (ScienceWorld), open-web navigation (Mind2Web) and competition mathematics (AMC23); the last also tests whether the pattern extends from action procedures to non-interactive reasoning strategies, so the trend is not an artifact of sequential control.

sections.heading: Backbones.
sections.text: Each method is run on the base model used in its experimental configuration: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct for SkillRL and Evolving-RL , and Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 for ReSkill and ARISE . Because the backbones differ, an absolute success rate characterizes a method together with its backbone rather than the method in isolation.

sections.heading: Evaluation sets.
sections.text: Evaluation uses the standard split of each benchmark—140 tasks on ALFWorld, 500 on WebShop, 155 validation points on ScienceWorld, and the standard evaluation splits of Mind2Web and DeepScaleR-AMC23—held fixed across every perturbation axis and every anchor, so the conditions being compared are paired at the level of individual tasks. The released configuration records the exact identifiers and sample counts for all six settings. Checkpoints are saved at a regular interval along each training trajectory; the exact anchor steps are shown in the corresponding fragility curves and verified full-results tables.

sections.heading: Repeats and error bars.
sections.text: Every anchor is evaluated repeatedly under six conditions—unperturbed and T1–T5—and reported with mean ± 1 \pm 1 s.d. The SkillRL and ReSkill settings use three repeats, and ReSkill -ScienceWorld uses five; repeat counts for Evolving-RL and ARISE are recorded in the released configuration. Repeats share the policy checkpoint and the same fixed set of perturbed banks and differ only in the rollout sampling seed. The delivered-pair report cards use the paired runs required to compute CR \mathrm{CR} , CR 0 \mathrm{CR}_{0} and RR \mathrm{RR} . Each setting comes from a single co-evolution run, so the bands quantify evaluation noise, not variability across training seeds.

sections.heading: Misleading-axis strength.
sections.text: For the four SkillRL / ReSkill settings, the misleading axis (T3) is applied at one strength per setting: the milder variant on the two ALFWorld settings and the stronger variant on WebShop and ScienceWorld. Both strengths were run in each of these four settings, and the one not reported in the main text is included in the full-results tables below.

sections.heading: H.3 Drop and Retention Are One Measurement on Two Scales
sections.text: The two quantities plotted in every dose figure are algebraically linked. Substituting the definition of Drop a \mathrm{Drop}_{a} into that of RP a \mathrm{RP}_{a} , RP a ​ ( t ) = SR ⁡ ( S a ∗ ) SR ⁡ ( S ∗ ) = SR ⁡ ( S ∗ ) − Drop a ​ ( t ) SR ⁡ ( S ∗ ) = 1 − Drop a ​ ( t ) SR ⁡ ( S ∗ ) , \mathrm{RP}_{a}(t)\;=\;\frac{\mathrm{SR}(S^{*}_{a})}{\mathrm{SR}(S^{*})}\;=\;\frac{\mathrm{SR}(S^{*})-\mathrm{Drop}_{a}(t)}{\mathrm{SR}(S^{*})}\;=\;1-\frac{\mathrm{Drop}_{a}(t)}{\mathrm{SR}(S^{*})}, (22) so retention is an affine transform of the drop: a flip about the horizontal axis, rescaled by 1 / SR ⁡ ( S ∗ ) 1/\mathrm{SR}(S^{*}) . Whenever the unperturbed rate is close to constant across anchors, the retention row is therefore an almost exact mirror image of the drop row, and the sole source of divergence between the two is variation in SR ⁡ ( S ∗ ) \mathrm{SR}(S^{*}) itself.

sections.text: On SkillRL -ALFWorld, RP T3 = 2.33 \mathrm{RP}_{\text{T3}}=2.33 at s0 and 3.38 3.38 at s5 : a misleading bank more than doubles the score of a policy that has not yet co-evolved with it. By s90 , RP T3 \mathrm{RP}_{\text{T3}} falls to 0.86 0.86 , while T5 moves from 4.17 4.17 to 0.82 0.82 . The same bank that initially obstructs the policy thus becomes a source of competence and, eventually, dependence. Across the six repeatedly evaluated settings, Figure 13 spans a relatively narrow competence range ( 28.5 % 28.5\% to 50.3 % 50.3\% ), so its drop and retention rows mirror each other almost perfectly. Figure 12 spans 5.2 % 5.2\% to 88.8 % 88.8\% ; there the small early denominators stretch retention onto a different scale altogether—T5 exceeds RP = 7 \mathrm{RP}=7 at the base anchor—and the two rows take visibly different shapes. We report both regardless, for opposite reasons: the absolute drop is what a deployment actually loses, while retention is the only one of the two that remains comparable across checkpoints—or across settings—whose ability differs by an order of magnitude. At a fixed anchor neither carries information the other lacks; what retention adds is comparability along the dose axis.

sections.heading: H.4 Dependence Mediates Fragility
sections.text: The dose curves plot fragility against the co-evolution step, but the step is only a proxy: what should actually govern how much a fixed corruption costs is how much the policy has come to rely on the bank. Figure 16 tests this directly. For every checkpoint we place one point at ( x , y ) (x,y) with x x the dependence—the drop in SR \mathrm{SR} when the bank is removed entirely (the no-skill / autonomy contrast)—and y y the fragility—the mean Drop \mathrm{Drop} over the five corruption tiers. Reading fragility against measured dependence removes the proxy, which matters because on SkillRL -WebShop the proxy fails outright: dependence there is not monotone in the step (it reverses across an s80 – s110 valley), so dependence and step are essentially uncorrelated, yet the dependence–fragility relation still holds. The two quantities lie on a single increasing line. Pooling the 32 32 checkpoints across both settings gives Spearman ρ = + 0.82 \rho=+0.82 ( 95 % 95\% CI [ + 0.68 , + 0.89 ] [+0.68,+0.89] , p = 7.4 × 10 − 9 p=7.4\times 10^{-9} ) and an ordinary-least-squares slope of + 0.20 +0.20 pp of fragility per pp of dependence ( 95 % 95\% bootstrap CI [ + 0.15 , + 0.28 ] [+0.15,+0.28] , excluding zero); each setting is individually significant ( SkillRL -ALFWorld ρ = + 0.78 \rho=+0.78 , p = 1.5 × 10 − 4 p=1.5\times 10^{-4} , n = 18 n=18 ; SkillRL -WebShop ρ = + 0.79 \rho=+0.79 , p = 7.9 × 10 − 4 p=7.9\times 10^{-4} , n = 14 n=14 ). The relation is not carried by a few extreme points: the shaded band is a 4000 4000 -sample bootstrap over anchors and stays narrow throughout. Crucially the line passes through the third quadrant. At the earliest checkpoints dependence is negative—removing the bank raises SR \mathrm{SR} , because the policy has not yet co-evolved to it—and there fragility is negative too: corrupting a bank the policy does not rely on helps . The same axis that predicts vulnerability at high dependence predicts a benefit at negative dependence, which is exactly the sign structure of Proposition 1 . Dependence, not elapsed training, is what fragility tracks; the dose effect of Section 3.2 is the composition of two links, training builds dependence and dependence creates fragility. sections.heading: How much of the drop is about wording?
sections.text: Comparing the two ends of the axis ordering gives a cheap diagnostic of surface-form dependence, κ = SR ⁡ ( S ∗ ) − SR ⁡ ( S T1 ∗ ) SR ⁡ ( S ∗ ) − SR ⁡ ( S T3 ∗ ) , \kappa\;=\;\frac{\mathrm{SR}(S^{*})-\mathrm{SR}(S^{*}_{\text{T1}})}{\mathrm{SR}(S^{*})-\mathrm{SR}(S^{*}_{\text{T3}})}, (23) the damage done by rewriting the words relative to the damage done by rewriting the strategy. A policy that reads a skill for its meaning should have κ \kappa near zero, since a synonymous rewrite costs it nothing while a wrong strategy costs it a great deal; a policy using the bank as a look-up table has κ \kappa near one or above. Measured values are κ = 0.78 \kappa=0.78 on SkillRL -ALFWorld and 2.14 2.14 on ReSkill -ScienceWorld; the latter exceeds one, meaning a meaning-preserving change hurts more than a wrong strategy does. On the other two SkillRL / ReSkill settings, the T3 axis does not lower the success rate below the peak, so κ \kappa is undefined (negative denominator). We report κ \kappa as a diagnostic and deliberately keep it out of Table 4 : the metric set is closed, and a ratio of two differences is too unstable near a small denominator to carry a pass line.

sections.heading: An observation, not a prediction.
sections.text: Injected skill text occupies an estimated 15% to 40% of the prompt across the four SkillRL / ReSkill settings included in this diagnostic, and those with the larger share are not systematically the ones with the higher worst-case rates. We record this because it is the first thing a reader will ask about and the measurement is nearly free, but it forms no part of the theory of Section 2 and we make no claim of a relationship.

sections.heading: H.6 T1 Meaning-Preservation Quality Assurance
sections.text: The T1 axis is defined as a meaning-preserving rewrite: the skill’s wording changes but its procedural content should not. Because the rewriting suite uses a language model rather than a deterministic operator, we verify this property with an independent, blinded audit whose design specifically defends against the two failure modes a reviewer would flag: the judge being biased toward the rewriter ( self-endorsement ) and the judge being insensitive (a rubber-stamp ).

sections.heading: Protocol.
sections.text: We audit all 190 T1 rewrites in the four SkillRL / ReSkill settings (91 on SkillRL -ALFWorld, 84 on SkillRL -WebShop, 7 on ReSkill -ScienceWorld, 8 on ReSkill -ALFWorld), so there is no sampling. Every pair is scored on a four-level rubric— equivalent , minor drift , meaning altered , reversed/unrelated —by two independent judges from different providers: qwen3-max (Alibaba) as the primary judge, cross-family with the rewriter (GPT-4o), and gpt-4o-2024-08-06 (OpenAI) as the secondary judge. The audit is blinded: pair order is shuffled, the original is randomly placed on the A or B side, and axis labels are kept only in an answer key. A human annotator re-checks 50% of the T1 pairs under the same blind protocol.

sections.heading: Judge validity: positive and negative controls.
sections.text: To confirm that the judges are neither over-eager nor over-lenient, the same blinded batch includes 20 identity pairs (a skill against itself) and 40 negative controls (a skill against its T2 or T3 rewrite, which by construction alter the prescribed action). Both judges rate all 20/20 identity pairs equivalent and all 40/40 negative controls as non-equivalent (mean rating ≤ 0.36 \leq 0.36 vs. 1.00 1.00 on identity), so they are not rubber stamps and not oversensitive.

sections.heading: Results.
sections.text: Under this test both judges rate 100% of the 190 T1 pairs as meaning-equivalent ( 0 / 190 0/190 altered; 95% Wilson CI [ 0.0 % , 1.9 % ] [0.0\%,1.9\%] ), with perfect binary agreement between judges (Cohen’s κ = 1.0 \kappa=1.0 ) and a four-level agreement of 95.8% (all disagreements fall within the negative controls, over the degree of alteration, never over its direction). The human re-check on 95 of the 190 T1 pairs (50%) concurs, with no meaning changes found. In these four settings, T1 rewrites therefore preserve meaning, and the corresponding consistency drop in Section 4.4 measures sensitivity to wording rather than rewrite noise.

sections.heading: H.7 The Cost in Standalone Ability
sections.text: If co-evolution builds dependence, the natural question is what that dependence is bought with. Figure 17 trains a pure-RL policy on SkillRL -ALFWorld with the skill mechanism disabled throughout (arm A, no bank at any step) and reads it against the co-evolved delivered checkpoint of the same setting, both with the bank present ( 84.1 % 84.1\% , n = 5 n=5 ) and with it removed ( 57.6 % 57.6\% , n = 5 n=5 ; step- 115 115 bank, evaluated on the eval_in_distribution split at temperature 0.4 0.4 ). Two things stand out. First, the co-evolved policy stripped of its bank scores 57.6 % 57.6\% , whereas a policy that never trained with skills reaches a last-five-checkpoint mean of 70.6 % 70.6\% and a peak of 87.5 % 87.5\% : co-evolution does not merely add a removable crutch, it leaves the underlying policy worse at acting alone than one that was never given the crutch. The dependence measured in Appendix H.4 is therefore not free—it is standalone ability traded away. Second, the pure-RL run is itself unstable: it peaks at 87.5 % 87.5\% near step 125 125 and then falls to 53.1 % 53.1\% by step 150 150 , with entropy and KL rising together over the same window (panels B, C). Neither training regime yields a monotone capability curve; the distinctive cost of co-evolution is the additional erosion of the skill-free policy. Yu, Xiaoming Wu, Jieping Ye Affiliation: Alibaba Token Hub, Alibaba Group Affiliation: The Hong Kong Polytechnic University Affiliation: University of Illinois at Chicago Abstract Skill–policy co-evolution—in which an agent’s policy model and its skill bank improve each other during training—is a promising paradigm for self-improving agents. Current evaluations score the co-evolved policy on the final bank it trained with (the delivered bank ). After deployment, however, skills may be rewritten, added or removed more frequently than the policy model is retrained, leaving the policy to operate on a drifted skill bank that neither the training objective nor existing evaluation protocols address. In this paper, we first establish, through theoretical and empirical analysis, that the fragility hidden by this blind spot is not incidental. The acceptance rule these methods share ( cooperative acceptance ) ties a policy’s competence to the bank it co-evolved with, leaving it fragile once skills drift, regardless of the implementation; empirically, sensitivity to skill drift grows as co-evolution training proceeds. We therefore introduce the CO -evolution D rift A udit ( CODA ), a deployment-oriented evaluation protocol that simulates skill drift and, alongside success rate under worst-case drift, introduces two new metrics: a consistency rate under meaning-preserving edits and a resistance rate to corrupted skills. Across four co-evolution methods and five benchmarks (six settings), worst-case success is 5–13 points below the peak measured for each delivered pair, erasing 52–93% of the delivered bank’s gain over the no-skill baseline. CODA thus reframes the target of co-evolution—from peak performance on the co-evolved bank to the ability to harness skills however they evolve—and provides a shared standard against which future methods can be audited. 1 Introduction Building agents that improve themselves is a central goal of current agent research, and co-evolving a skill library with a policy is one of the most promising routes ( Xia et al., 2026a ; He et al., 2026 ) . The agent solves tasks, distills the experience into reusable skills, and uses those skills to strengthen its policy in turn, so competence compounds over rounds. A recent line of methods ( Shi et al., 2026 ; Li et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026b ; Yang et al., 2026a ; Lin et al., 2026 ) follows exactly this recipe: it iterates the policy and the skill bank together during training and reports large gains on agent benchmarks. Each ultimately delivers a pair—a co-evolved policy and its final skill bank (the delivered bank )—and reports the policy’s task success on that bank. However, current evaluation is disconnected from deployment: it assumes that the skill bank remains fixed after training. Real skill banks are non-stationary: skills are rewritten, entries are added or removed, and versions coexist, often changing faster than the policy is retrained. A deployed policy therefore typically runs on a bank that has drifted from the one it was delivered with, yet existing protocols do not test whether performance is maintained. A few works note this brittleness ( Liu et al., 2026d ; Hebbar et al., 2026 ) but offer neither a systematic measurement nor a causal account. We argue that the blind spot conceals a property of the training objective, not an incidental evaluation artifact. Co-evolution repeatedly adapts the policy and bank into a mutually specialized pair, while evaluation rewards exactly that pairing. The policy is therefore optimized for its delivered bank rather than for transferable skill use. We establish this in two ways. Theoretically, we prove that the shared acceptance rule—retaining a skill update only when it helps the current policy—places the delivered pair at a peak over candidate banks, so rewriting the delivered skills cannot improve the policy and usually degrades its performance (Section 2 ). Empirically, using the proposed co-evolution fragility curve , we show that sensitivity to skill drift increases as training proceeds in five of six settings (Section 3 ). We call this the co-evolution trap (Figure 1 ): the process that raises peak performance also creates sensitivity to bank drift. Figure 1: The skill–policy co-evolution trap (conceptual illustration) . (1) Training : The policy and skill bank co-evolve round by round, and evaluation reports the peak reached by the resulting delivered pair. (2) Deployment : The skill bank continues to evolve while the policy remains fixed. Because the policy is specialized to its delivered bank, its performance degrades as the bank drifts. (3) Goal : An ideally co-evolved policy that retains its performance as skills evolve. Establishing the problem exposes a second gap: existing evaluations cannot measure it, because they report only one success rate on the fixed delivered bank. We therefore introduce the CO -evolution D rift A udit ( CODA ), a deployment-oriented protocol for auditing post-deployment skill drift under controlled conditions. CODA supplements the conventional peak success rate with worst-case success and two new metrics—a consistency rate under meaning-preserving edits and a resistance rate to corrupted skills. Across four methods and five benchmarks (six settings), worst-case success is 5–13 points below the peak measured for each delivered pair, erasing 52–93% of the delivered bank’s gain over the no-skill baseline, so the reported peak overstates the competence a deployment can rely on. CODA thus reframes the target of co-evolution—from achieving peak performance on the bank a method co-evolved with to using skills reliably as they keep changing—and we release it as a common standard for auditing future methods. Our main contributions are summarized as follows: • We expose a trap in skill–policy co-evolution : current evaluations measure fit to a fixed delivered bank, leaving performance under deployment-time bank change unmeasured. • We theoretically and empirically demonstrate its mechanism and signature: under cooperative acceptance and candidate coverage, no covered rewrite improves the delivered policy; empirically, 18/18 endpoint pairs obey this prediction and fragility grows along training in five of six settings. • We propose a deployment-oriented evaluation protocol , CODA, reporting worst-case success under tested content-level drift, consistency under meaning-preserving edits, and resistance to corrupted skills, making the deployment robustness of the delivered policy–bank pair measurable. 2 Why Co-evolution Favors Specialization over Robustness Problem setting. A task x x is drawn from a distribution D D , a skill bank S S lies in a space 𝒮 \mathcal{S} , and a policy π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , S ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,S) maps both to a distribution over action sequences, with skills entering as text in its context. Methods optimize and report the expected return J ( θ , S ) = 𝔼 x ∼ D [ R ( π θ ( ⋅ ∣ x , S ) ) ] , J(\theta,S)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}\!\left[R\!\left(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,S)\right)\right], (1) where R R is a binary success indicator, so J J is the reported success rate. We fold skill selection into π θ \pi_{\theta} , making J J a function of the bank as a whole. Co-evolution alternates a policy step , which improves θ \theta against the current bank, and a bank step , which proposes banks by rewriting, adding or removing skills and retains one through an acceptance test. After T T rounds, it delivers ( θ ∗ , S ∗ ) (\theta^{*},S^{*}) and reports J ⁡ ( θ ∗ , S ∗ ) J(\theta^{*},S^{*}) as its peak return —the de facto objective for comparing these methods. 2.1 A Unified View and the Premise It Reveals Current methods differ in update cadence , bank growth , validation gate and injection mechanism (Table 1 ; definitions in Appendix C ). Across these choices, they share two patterns. First, they optimize and report peak return on the bank they co-evolved with. Second, their gates favor banks that serve the current policy, whether through reward thresholds, sampled-return comparisons or posteriors over competing versions. What the field lacks, however, is not another method—new update rules or acceptance tests—but a way to measure the failure: a shared standard that scores how well a delivered policy holds up when its bank changes, comparably across methods. We therefore introduce CODA, a protocol that audits the one artifact every method ships—a co-evolved policy and its delivered bank—and reports its robustness to skill drift on a common footing. 4.1 Design and the Shared Rewriting Suite CODA audits only the delivered pair—a co-evolved policy and its delivered bank—plus the shared suite, and assigns scores only to quantities with a predefined direction, so the metric set stays closed; the design rationale (checkpoint-freeness, the direction-first rule, and why diagnostics such as the surface-form ratio κ \kappa of Appendix H.5 are excluded) is in Appendix E . The suite is the part of this paper meant to outlive it, under one hard rule: rewriting is performed by the released suite, not by the party under evaluation —an evaluation whose conditions the evaluated party controls is not an evaluation. For the content-level axes T1–T3, retrieval is run once on the unperturbed bank and only the content of the selected skills is rewritten; the suite pins the rewriting model and its sampling, releases the perturbed banks rather than a script, preserves bank structure, and reports the edit strength it produced. A growing family of methods co-evolves a skill library with the policy, including SkillRL ( Xia et al., 2026a ) , ReSkill ( He et al., 2026 ) , Skill1 ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , ARISE ( Li et al., 2026 ) , SAPO ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) , and SkillMaster ( Yang et al., 2026a ) . These methods differ in update cadence, library growth, validation gates, and skill injection (Table 1 ), yet share the same evaluation premise: the co-evolved policy is tested on its delivered bank. We introduce no new member of this family; instead, we examine this shared premise and its consequences under deployment-time skill drift. Agent robustness under skill drift. Robustness evaluations for language agents typically perturb the task side of the interaction—instructions, observations, tool outputs, or environment dynamics. We instead perturb the agent’s own procedural knowledge, which task-side benchmarks treat as fixed. Recent work documents that skill libraries drift and that agent performance can degrade accordingly ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ) , that skills may harm rather than help ( Tank and Nama, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) , and that self-evolution is not always faithful ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Lv et al., 2026 ) . Other approaches repair skills post hoc or construct more drift-tolerant skills ( Liu et al., 2026c ; Park et al., 2026 ; Shao et al., 2026 ) ; by contrast, we audit the delivered policy’s dependence on whichever bank it encounters. This setting also resembles zero-shot coordination ( Hu et al., 2020 ) , with the skill bank acting as a co-evolved partner that may change after training. Appendix B provides further discussion. 6 Conclusion This work shifts the evaluation of skill–policy co-evolution from performance on a single delivered pair to robustness under realistic deployment-time skill drift. Our analysis identifies cooperative acceptance as a source of dependence on the co-evolved bank, while the co-evolution fragility curve shows that this dependence can strengthen over training. CODA operationalizes these findings by auditing whether a delivered policy remains consistent under benign rewrites and resists incomplete or misleading skills. The delivered peak is therefore informative but insufficient: future methods should preserve its gains while learning to interpret, reject, and adapt to skills as the bank evolves. L1 Rewriting is not bit-reproducible. A language model rewriting a skill is not a deterministic operator: pinned model versions, pinned sampling, and released perturbed banks reduce the variance a re-runner faces but do not remove it. If the bank was written by the same model family that later rewrites it, the measured fragility may be optimistically low. L2 We diagnose but do not fix.
