Appendix B Extended Related Work Skill–policy co-evolution. A growing family of methods lets an agent distill task experience into reusable skills and then trains the policy on the enlarged bank ( Liu et al., 2026a ; Zou et al., 2026 ; Yang et al., 2026b ; Feng et al., 2026 ) . SkillRL ( Xia et al., 2026a ) distills successful trajectories into skills that are added to a monotonically growing library and gated by reward on sampled rollouts. ReSkill ( He et al., 2026 ) caps the library at a fixed size and uses Thompson sampling to decide which incumbent a new candidate should replace. Skill1 ( Shi et al., 2026 ) jointly optimizes the policy and bank end-to-end, admitting skills from trajectories that already succeed. ARISE ( Li et al., 2026 ) evolves a two-tier hierarchy of intrinsic skills under a hierarchical reward. SAPO ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) admits a skill only when its estimated marginal utility to the current policy is positive. SkillMaster ( Yang et al., 2026a ) lets the policy itself score candidates, retaining high-scoring ones into a managed library. These methods differ in cadence, library growth, validation gate, and injection mechanism (Table 1 ; Appendix C gives the full classification). What they do not differ in is how success is reported: the co-evolved policy is run on the delivered bank and a task success rate is given. Surveys chart this space ( Zhou et al., 2026 ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Ren et al., 2026 ) , and recent variants push co-evolution to test-time ( Mao et al., 2026 ) , self-play ( Huang et al., 2026 ) , and deployment-time meta-learning ( Xia et al., 2026b ) . We contribute no new member of this family. Our object of study is the family itself—specifically, the one premise that survives all of their design disagreements. Agent robustness and adversarial co-evolution. Work on robustness for language agents perturbs the task side of the interaction—instructions, observations, tool outputs, environment dynamics—and asks whether performance survives. We perturb a different thing: the agent’s own store of procedural knowledge, which no task-side benchmark touches because it is normally treated as part of the agent rather than part of the environment. Concurrently, a cluster of works documents that skill libraries drift and that agents degrade under that drift ( Zhang et al., 2026a ; Chen et al., 2026b ; Liu et al., 2026b ; Chen et al., 2026a ) , that skills can hurt as often as they help ( Tank and Nama, 2026 ; Yu et al., 2026 ) , and that self-evolution is not always faithful ( Zhao et al., 2026 ; Lv et al., 2026 ) . These diagnose the symptom; none ties it to the co-evolution objective or measures it on the delivered artifact. SkillRevise ( Liu et al., 2026c ) repairs skills post hoc, and GenDa ( Park et al., 2026 ) with programmatic skill induction ( Shao et al., 2026 ) build drift-tolerant skills from the skill side; we instead audit the policy’s dependence on whatever bank it is handed. The closest conceptual relative is zero-shot coordination ( Hu et al., 2020 ) , where a policy trained with one partner must act with another it never co-evolved with; our setting is the single-agent analog, with the skill library in the role of the partner that changed. A separate line evolves an adversary alongside the learner, in game-theoretic heuristic discovery ( Ke et al., 2026 ) or attacker–defender safety training ( Wen et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2025 ) , and reports robustness gains . This is not a counterexample to Proposition 1 but a confirmation of its premise read in reverse: those methods accept a candidate precisely when it lowers the current policy’s return, so the sign in Assumption 1 is flipped and the conclusion flips with it. Appendix D.5 works this through, and the comparison is instructive rather than competitive: it locates the fragility in the acceptance rule rather than in co-evolution as such. Standardized perturbation suites. CODA belongs to a tradition of fixed perturbation suites applied to models their designers did not build: corruption benchmarks in vision ( Hendrycks and Dietterich, 2019 ) and behavioral test suites in NLP ( Ribeiro et al., 2020 ) both consist of a released operator, a reporting convention, and the finding that published systems fail more than their headline numbers suggest. We follow that template on the skill side. One difference must be stated rather than glossed over: those operators are deterministic algorithms that reproduce bit-for-bit, whereas rewriting a skill with a language model does not. We narrow the gap: we pin the rewriting model, its version and its sampling parameters; we ship the domain context so nothing is left to the user; and we release the perturbed banks alongside the suite (Section 4.1 ). We do not close it, though— Section 6 lists it first among the limitations. Appendix C Classification of Existing Methods The four axes of Table 1 are defined as follows. Update cadence determines how the two steps interleave, from strictly alternating through near-synchronous to jointly optimized. The validation gate determines how a candidate bank is admitted: no test at all, an improvement test on sampled rollouts, or a posterior test such as Thompson sampling. Library growth is either monotone, so that skills accumulate, or capped, so that admission displaces an incumbent. The injection mechanism determines what reaches the context at inference: a batch selected by task category, or a small subset triggered per step. We now place each surveyed method on these axes and state its acceptance rule—the property that Assumption 1 abstracts. In every case the gate admits a candidate bank only when it does not lower (and usually strictly raises) the current policy’s return, however differently that test is implemented. • SkillRL ( Xia et al., 2026a ) : alternating cadence, monotone growth, batch top- k k injection. A distilled skill is admitted whenever it does not reduce reward on sampled rollouts and is never removed thereafter, so the retained bank is the reward-non-decreasing one. • ReSkill ( He et al., 2026 ) : near-synchronous cadence, library capped at eight, per-step injection. A candidate is validated by Thompson sampling and kept only if its posterior return improves on the incumbent it would displace. • SAPO ( Zhang et al., 2026b ) : near-synchronous cadence, two-tier capped growth, reranked injection. A skill enters only when its estimated marginal utility to the current policy is positive. • Skill1 ( Shi et al., 2026 ) : joint optimization, monotone growth, log-probability injection. Skills are distilled from trajectories that already succeed ( r = 1 r{=}1 ) and trained jointly with the policy, so what is retained is exactly what supported a return the policy did not lose. • ARISE ( Li et al., 2026 ) : joint optimization, two-tier growth, log-probability injection. Intrinsic skills are evolved under a hierarchical reward and retained on improvement of that reward. • SkillMaster ( Yang et al., 2026a ) : near-synchronous cadence, policy-managed growth and injection. The policy itself scores candidate skills and retains the high-scoring ones, i.e. those that raise its own return. • Evolving-RL ( Fan et al., 2026 ) : joint optimization, monotone growth, batch injection. A skill is admitted end-to-end when it clears a reward threshold on the current policy. • COSPLAY ( Wu et al., 2026 ) : near-synchronous cadence, lifecycle-managed growth, per-step injection. Skills pass a contract-verification step and are retained over their lifecycle while they continue to serve the policy’s return. The gates differ in form—an improvement test on rollouts, a Thompson posterior, a marginal-utility check, a reward threshold, a policy score, a contract—but all favor skills that serve the current policy. Assumption 1 idealizes this shared selection bias. Proposition 1 is model-agnostic but additionally requires the candidate-coverage condition of Assumption 2 ; it therefore applies conditionally rather than automatically to the eight surveyed methods.
